title: CSC3710 2026-09-17 — Regular Sets and Regular Expressions

questions.q: Over Σ = {a, b}, which sets are \*\*basis\*\* elements in the recursive definition of the regular sets?
questions.explain: The basis is ∅, {λ}, and {x} for every symbol x ∈ Σ, so over {a, b}: ∅, {λ}, {a}, {b}. {a, b} is regular, but only after one union step; {aa} needs a concatenation step.

questions.q: Which list is exactly the set of operations allowed in the recursive step for regular sets?
questions.explain: The recursive step allows X ∪ Y, XY and X\*, and nothing else. Intersection and complement do preserve regularity (a later theorem), but they are not part of the definition.

questions.q: What is the job of the \*\*closure\*\* clause in the definition of the regular sets?
choices: It says the regular sets are closed under intersection
It says a set is regular only if it can be built from the basis by finitely many applications of the recursive step
It says every set of strings over Σ is regular
It says the Kleene star may only be applied once
questions.explain: Basis and recursive step say which sets \*are\* regular; closure says \*no other\* sets are: a set is regular only if some finite number of applications of the recursive step builds it from the basis.

questions.q: ∅ and {λ} are the same set, because both contain "nothing".
questions.explain: ∅ has zero elements. {λ} has one element, the empty string. They behave differently: X∅ = ∅ but X{λ} = X. They are listed separately in the basis for this reason.

questions.q: What is {a, ab}{b, λ}?
questions.explain: XY = {uv | u ∈ X, v ∈ Y}: a·b = ab, a·λ = a, ab·b = abb, ab·λ = ab. Duplicates collapse, giving {a, ab, abb}.

questions.q: For sets of strings, XY = YX always.
questions.explain: Order matters: {a}{b} = {ab} but {b}{a} = {ba}. The recursive step covers both XY and YX because X and Y are arbitrary, but they are generally different sets.

questions.q: For every set X of strings, λ ∈ X\*.
questions.explain: X\* = X⁰ ∪ X¹ ∪ …, and X⁰ = {λ}. So λ is in X\* for every X, including X = ∅.

questions.q: Which equalities of \*\*sets\*\* are true?
questions.explain: {λ}\* = {λ} (copies of λ give λ). ∅\* = {λ} because ∅⁰ = {λ} and ∅ⁿ = ∅ for n ≥ 1. X∅ = ∅ (nothing to pair with). ∅\* is not ∅, since it contains λ.

questions.topic: Operation need not create new set
questions.q: Applying the recursive step to a regular set always produces a \*\*new\*\* regular set, different from the ones used.
questions.explain: Not necessarily. {λ} is regular by the basis and {λ}\* is regular by the star step, but {λ}\* = {λ}. Likewise X ∪ X = X.

questions.q: For a set X of strings, which is X⁺?
questions.explain: X⁺ = X¹ ∪ X² ∪ … = XX\*: one or more concatenated elements of X. It contains λ only if λ ∈ X.

questions.q: In the proof that L = {a, b}\*{aaa} is regular, which step is justified by \*\*union\*\*?
questions.explain: {a, b} is built from the basis sets {a} and {b} by union. {aa} and {aaa} come from concatenation, {a, b}\* from the star, and the final set from concatenating {a, b}\* with {aaa}.

questions.q: The last step of the proof concatenates {a, b}\* and {aaa}. Why does the order matter?
choices: {a, b}\*{aaa} ends with aaa, but {aaa}{a, b}\* starts with aaa
The star must always be applied last
Only the order of the basis steps matters
questions.explain: {a, b}\*{aaa} is the strings that \*\*end\*\* with aaa; {aaa}{a, b}\* would be those that \*\*start\*\* with aaa. Concatenation is not commutative, so the order you cite must match the target set.

questions.q: In a "prove this set is regular" table, the steps may be done in any order, as long as every set used in a step has already been shown to be regular.
questions.explain: For example you can build {a, b}\* before {aaa}. What matters is that every justification cites earlier rows (or the basis).

questions.q: Which construction proves that the strings over {a, b} that \*\*begin with bb\*\* form a regular set?
questions.explain: The set is {bb}{a, b}\*: {b} (basis), {bb} = {b}{b} (concatenation), {a}, {a, b} (union), {a, b}\* (star), then {bb}{a, b}\* (concatenation in that order). Option 1 is ends-with-bb; option 3 only allows b's afterwards; option 4 is only {bb}.

questions.q: After building {a, b}\*{aaa} from the basis in 7 justified steps, which clause lets you conclude that the set is regular?
choices: Finitely many applications of the recursive step starting from the basis (recursive step + closure)
The fact that the set is infinite
questions.explain: The recursive step says each individual step produces a regular set; the closure clause frames the result: a set obtained from the basis by finitely many applications of the recursive step is exactly what a regular set is. (Most books accept citing either; the key point is the construction is finite and every step is justified.)

questions.q: Which strings belong to {a, b}\*{aaa}?
questions.explain: Any string (including λ) followed by aaa: aaa = λ·aaa, baaa = b·aaa, abaaa = ab·aaa. aab and aaab do not end in aaa.

questions.q: A set is listed as {ba, baa, bab, baaa, baab, baba, babb, …}. Which regular-set construction describes it?
questions.explain: Every string starts with ba and is followed by any string over {a, b}: {b}{a}{a, b}\*. The other options either end with ba or force a fixed third symbol.

questions.q: What is the precedence of the regular-expression operators, from most binding to least?
questions.explain: Star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union — like exponent, multiplication, addition in arithmetic.

questions.q: How is ab\* read?
questions.explain: The star applies only to the symbol immediately before it: a(b\*). It describes {a, ab, abb, …}, not (ab)\* = {λ, ab, abab, …}.

questions.q: How is ab ∪ c read?
questions.explain: Concatenation binds tighter than union: (ab) ∪ c, describing {ab, c}. a(b ∪ c) would be {ab, ac}.

questions.q: Which full parenthesization matches (ab)\*a ∪ b\*?
questions.explain: Star first, then concatenation, then union: ((ab)\*a) ∪ (b\*). Its shortest strings are λ (from b\*), a, b.

questions.q: What are the three shortest strings described by a ∪ b\*a?
questions.explain: Read as a ∪ ((b\*)a). b\*a gives a, ba, bba, …; the separate a is the same string a, which a set lists once. So a, ba, bba. λ is not in the set: b\*a always ends with a.

questions.q: Which expressions are equal to u⁺ for every regular expression u?
questions.explain: u⁺ = uu\* = u\*u (one or more copies). u\* also contains λ even when u doesn't, and u ∪ λ allows at most one copy.

questions.q: What does (a ∪ b)³ abbreviate?
questions.explain: uⁿ is u concatenated with itself n times, so (a ∪ b)³ = (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)(a ∪ b): all 8 strings of length exactly 3. It is not the union of lengths up to 3, and not a³ ∪ b³.

questions.q: By convention, u⁰ is
questions.explain: u⁰ = λ, matching X⁰ = {λ} for sets. That is also why u\* = u⁰ ∪ u¹ ∪ … always contains λ.

questions.q: In the definition of regular expressions, the regular expression \*\*λ\*\* corresponds to which regular set?
questions.explain: Regular expressions mirror regular sets clause by clause with the braces dropped: ∅ ↔ ∅, λ ↔ {λ}, a ↔ {a}.

questions.q: In a regular expression viewed as a pattern, which roles do concatenation, star and ∪ play?
questions.explain: Concatenation fixes order (a string from u followed by a string from v), the star permits repetition, and ∪ permits selection between alternatives.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the course's preferred wording?
choices: ab\*b is an element of {ab, abb, …}
questions.explain: An expression is notation; a set is a set. Say the expression \*\*describes\*\* the set. "=" is reserved for two expressions that describe the same set. (Writing "=" between an expression and a set is accepted on a test but discouraged.)

questions.q: Which description of a\*b is exactly right?
choices: One or more a's followed by a b
Zero or more a's followed by exactly one b
questions.explain: a\*b is zero or more a's followed by exactly one b. "Ends with b" is too loose (abab ends with b but isn't in it); "one or more a's" wrongly excludes b.

questions.q: ab\*b describes the same set as which expression?
questions.explain: b\* followed by b gives b, bb, bbb, …, i.e. b⁺. So ab\*b = ab⁺: an a followed by one or more b's.

questions.q: What are the shortest strings, in order, of (ab\*b)\*?
questions.explain: (ab\*b)\* = (ab⁺)\*: repeat blocks ab, abb, abbb, …. The outer star gives λ; then ab (2), abb (3), then abab and abbb (4). Forgetting λ was the mistake made in class.

questions.q: Which strings belong to the set described by (ab⁺)\* but \*\*not\*\* to the set described by ab⁺?
questions.explain: ab⁺ is a single a followed by b's. (ab⁺)\* allows λ and any sequence of blocks: abab = ab·ab, abbab = abb·ab. abbb is in both.

questions.q: Which length-3 strings belong to the set described by a\*bb\*?
questions.explain: a\*bb\* = a\*b⁺: zero or more a's, then one or more b's. Length 3: aab, abb, bbb. Don't forget bbb (no a's). aba has an a after a b; aaa has no b.

questions.q: Which strings belong to the set described by (aba)\*?
questions.explain: There is only one block, aba, so strings are λ, aba, abaaba, …. abaab is not a sequence of aba blocks.

questions.q: Which strings belong to the set described by a(a ∪ bb)\*?
questions.explain: Split into the leading a and then blocks a / bb. aabbbbbbaabb = a|a|bb|bb|bb|a|a|bb ✓; abbaabb = a|bb|a|a|bb ✓; abb = a|bb ✓. aab leaves a single b; abab has a single b before an a; bba doesn't start with a.

questions.q: Which is an equivalent description of the set described by a(a ∪ bb)\*?
choices: Strings that start with a and have an even number of symbols
Strings that start with a in which every run of b's has even length
Strings with an even number of b's
Strings that start with a and end with bb
questions.explain: Blocks a and bb in any order mean every maximal run of b's has even length, and the leading a forces the string to start with a (so it is non-empty).

questions.q: Which statements about (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)\*bbb are true?
choices: It describes the strings that end with bbb and have length at least 4
bbb belongs to the set it describes
bbbb belongs to the set it describes
questions.explain: (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)\* = (a ∪ b)⁺, so the expression is (a ∪ b)⁺bbb: strings ending in bbb with at least one symbol before it, i.e. length ≥ 4. bbb itself (length 3) is not in it; bbbb is.

questions.q: Which set does ab ∪ aba\* describe?
questions.explain: The star applies only to the last a: aba\* = ab·a\* = {ab, aba, abaa, …}. Union with {ab} adds nothing new.

questions.q: Which strings of length ≤ 4 belong to the set described by (a ∪ bb)\*b?
questions.explain: A block sequence from (a ∪ bb)\* followed by b. Length 1: b; 2: ab; 3: aab, bbb; 4: aaab, abbb, bbab. bb (length 2) would need the blocks to produce a single b, which is impossible.

questions.q: Why does the instructor avoid asking for \*\*word descriptions\*\* of regular expressions on tests?
choices: They are always longer than the expression
They are risky and subjective; answers vary too much
questions.explain: Word descriptions are subjective and everyone phrases them differently, so they are hard to grade. Tests focus on shortest strings and "does this string belong to the set described by…" questions.

questions.q: List the three shortest strings of ab\* ∪ b, separated by commas (use shortlex order).
questions.explain: Read as (a(b\*)) ∪ b: a(b\*) gives a, ab, abb, …; plus b. Shortlex: a, b, ab.

questions.q: You are asked whether two regular expressions are equivalent. What should you try first?
choices: Look for a string that belongs to one set but not the other
Count the number of stars in each
Compare the lengths of the two expressions
questions.explain: Look for a counterexample: a string in one set but not the other. A single counterexample proves the sets differ. If you can't find one, suspect equality and then prove it (both inclusions, or identities).

questions.q: (a ∪ bb ∪ aa)\* and (a ∪ bb)\* are equivalent.
questions.explain: The block aa is redundant: it can be built from two copies of the block a. Every string of one is a string of the other.

questions.q: Which string is a counterexample showing (a ∪ bb)\* and (a ∪ b)\* are not equivalent?
questions.explain: b belongs to the set described by (a ∪ b)\* but not to (a ∪ bb)\*, where b's only come in pairs. λ, bb and abb belong to both.

questions.q: Which strings are counterexamples showing (ab)\* and a\*b\* are not equivalent?
questions.explain: a and aab are in a\*b\* but not (ab)\* (whose non-empty strings are ab repeated). abab is in (ab)\* but not a\*b\* (a b is followed by an a). λ and ab are in both.

questions.q: Are a\*(a ∪ b)\* and (a ∪ b)\* equivalent?
choices: Yes: choose λ from a\*, and anything over {a,b} is in (a ∪ b)\*
No: a\*(a ∪ b)\* has more strings
questions.explain: Yes. Every string in a\*(a ∪ b)\* is a string over {a, b}; conversely, any w over {a, b} is λ·w with λ from a\*. (Instance of identity 12: u\*(u ∪ v)\* = (u ∪ v)\*.)

questions.q: Two infinite sets differ. Which wording does the course recommend?
choices: The first set has more elements
There are strings that belong to the first set but not to the second
The first set is infinite and the second is not
questions.explain: With infinite sets, "more elements" is misleading (sizes of infinite sets are counterintuitive). Say there are elements that belong to one set but not the other.

questions.q: Checking that two expressions agree on every string up to length 5 proves they are equivalent.
questions.explain: Agreement on short strings is evidence, not proof: a difference might appear at a longer length. To prove equivalence you show both inclusions or use identities. Only non-equivalence is proven by one example.

questions.q: In the algebraic proof ab ∪ aba\* = aba\*, the step abλ ∪ aba\* = ab(λ ∪ aa\*) uses which identity?
questions.explain: Factoring ab out on the left is distributivity: u(v ∪ w) = uv ∪ uw. The next step uses λ ∪ aa\* = λ ∪ a⁺ = a\*.

questions.q: Which is a correct simplification of ab ∪ ab(b)\* ∪ λ\*ab?
questions.explain: λ\*ab = λab = ab; ab ∪ ab = ab; and ab already belongs to abb\* (take λ from b\*), so the whole thing is abb\* = ab⁺. Not ab\* (that contains a), and not ab.

questions.q: Which are valid regular-expression identities?
questions.explain: ∅u = ∅; λu = u; u\* = (u\*)\*; (uv)\*u = u(vu)\* all hold. (u ∪ v)\* = u\* ∪ v\* is false: ab is in the left side but not the right.

questions.q: Give the shortest counterexample (over {a, b}) showing (a ∪ b)\* ≠ a\* ∪ b\*. If several tie, give the first in shortlex order.
questions.explain: a\* ∪ b\* contains only strings of a single letter. The shortest mixed strings are ab and ba (length 2); ab comes first in shortlex order.

questions.q: Why is (a ∪ b)\*aa(a ∪ b)\* ∪ (a ∪ b)\*aaa(a ∪ b)\* equivalent to (a ∪ b)\*aa(a ∪ b)\*?
choices: Every string containing aaa already contains aa
aaa and aa have the same length
They are not equivalent: aaa is a counterexample
questions.explain: Any string containing aaa also contains aa, so the second term's strings already belong to the first. A union with a subset adds nothing.

questions.q: If a regular expression contains a Kleene star, the set it describes is infinite.
questions.explain: Counterexamples: λ\* describes {λ} and ∅\* describes {λ}. For example aaλ\* describes {aa}.

questions.q: A regular expression with no Kleene star always describes a finite set.
questions.explain: Without a star it is built from finitely many basis pieces by union and concatenation, and those operations on finite sets give finite sets.

questions.q: For a regular expression to describe an infinite set, a Kleene star is
questions.explain: Necessary (no star ⇒ finite, so infinite ⇒ some star) but not sufficient (λ\* and ∅\* are finite).

questions.q: Which expressions describe \*\*finite\*\* sets?
questions.explain: aaλ\* = {aa}; ∅\* = {λ}; (∅\* ∪ a)b = (λ ∪ a)b = {b, ab}; (λ ∪ ∅)\* = λ\* = {λ}. (a ∪ λ)\* contains a, aa, aaa, … — infinite, because a is a non-empty string.

questions.q: When does u\* describe an infinite set?
choices: Exactly when u describes at least one non-empty string
questions.explain: Exactly when u describes at least one non-empty string: repeating it gives strings of unbounded length. If u describes only ∅ or {λ}, u\* is {λ}.

questions.q: As a regular expression, ∅\* simplifies to
questions.explain: ∅\* = λ (identity 3): as sets, ∅\* = {λ} since ∅⁰ = {λ}.

questions.q: If a regular set is infinite, every regular expression that describes it contains a star.
questions.explain: This is the contrapositive of "no star ⇒ finite". Every expression for an infinite set must contain at least one star.

questions.q: Which expressions describe the strings over {a, b, c} of length exactly three?
choices: (a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)
questions.explain: A union listing all 27 strings works, as do (a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c) and (a ∪ b ∪ c)³. There is no preferred form. aaa ∪ bbb ∪ ccc misses the mixed strings such as aab.

questions.q: Which expression describes the strings over {a, b, c} of length less than three?
choices: (a ∪ b ∪ c ∪ λ)(a ∪ b ∪ c ∪ λ)
a ∪ b ∪ c ∪ aa ∪ ab ∪ ac ∪ ba ∪ bb ∪ bc ∪ ca ∪ cb ∪ cc
questions.explain: Each factor (a ∪ b ∪ c ∪ λ) contributes one symbol or nothing, giving lengths 0, 1, 2 (13 strings, including λ). (a ∪ b ∪ c)² gives only length 2; the third option forgets λ.

questions.q: How many strings over {a, b, c} have length less than three?
questions.explain: 1 (λ) + 3 (length 1) + 9 (length 2) = 13.

questions.q: Let s = (a ∪ b ∪ c). Which describe the strings of length \*\*greater than three\*\*?
questions.explain: Greater than three means at least 4. s⁴s\* and s³s⁺ both force at least four symbols. s³s\* allows length 3; s⁴s⁺ forces at least 5.

questions.q: A student writes (a ∪ b)\*aa(a ∪ b)\*bb(a ∪ b)\* for "contains both aa and bb". Which string shows it is wrong?
questions.explain: It only covers aa before bb. bbaa contains both but is not produced. Fix: union with (a ∪ b)\*bb(a ∪ b)\*aa(a ∪ b)\*.

questions.q: Why is (a ∪ b)\*(aa ∪ bb)(a ∪ b)\*(aa ∪ bb)(a ∪ b)\* wrong for "contains both aa and bb"?
choices: It accepts bbbb, which contains no aa
It is not a valid regular expression
questions.explain: Each (aa ∪ bb) slot chooses independently, so both can pick bb: bbbb belongs to the set but has no aa. Moving the union inside loses the "and" requirement; the set is too big.

questions.q: (a ∪ b)\*ab(a ∪ b)\*ba(a ∪ b)\* ∪ (a ∪ b)\*ba(a ∪ b)\*ab(a ∪ b)\* is proposed for "contains both ab and ba". What is wrong?
choices: It misses aba and bab, where ab and ba overlap
It accepts abab, which lacks ba
questions.explain: The pattern forces ab and ba to be disjoint, so every string has length ≥ 4. But in aba (and bab) the two substrings overlap on the middle letter. Add (a ∪ b)\*aba(a ∪ b)\* ∪ (a ∪ b)\*bab(a ∪ b)\*.

questions.topic: Short form for ab and ba
questions.q: a⁺b⁺a(a ∪ b)\* ∪ b⁺a⁺b(a ∪ b)\* describes the strings over {a, b} containing both ab and ba.
questions.explain: Containing both ab and ba means the letter changes at least twice: a run of one letter, a run of the other, then the first letter again, then anything.

questions.q: Which describe the strings over {a, b} of length ≥ 2 in which all a's come before all b's (all-a and all-b strings allowed)?
questions.explain: a⁺b⁺ ∪ aa⁺ ∪ bb⁺ and a⁺b⁺ ∪ aaa\* ∪ bbb\* are the same answer (aa⁺ = aaa\*). a\*(aa ∪ ab ∪ bb)b\* works via the length-2 core. a⁺b⁺ misses aa, bb; a\*b\* includes λ, a, b.

questions.q: What is wrong with aa\*b\* ∪ a\*bb\* for the "length ≥ 2, all a's before all b's" language?
choices: It includes a and b, which have length 1
questions.explain: Each side can produce a single letter (a from aa\*b\*, b from a\*bb\*), so length-1 strings sneak in. Counterexample: a.

questions.q: Every regular language has one preferred regular expression, and answers in other forms lose credit.
questions.explain: There is no unique or preferred expression, and no rule about when to stop simplifying: "if it's good, it's good." A DFA-derived expression can look very different from a hand-written one.

questions.topic: Length at most two, no c
questions.q: Which describes the strings over {a, b, c} of length at most two that contain no c?
questions.explain: No c means the alphabet is effectively {a, b}; each of two positions is a, b or nothing. (a ∪ b)² misses λ, a, b; (a ∪ b)\* is unbounded.

questions.topic: Shortest strings with aa and bb
questions.q: Which are the shortest strings of the correct expression for "contains both aa and bb"?
questions.explain: Both substrings need 4 symbols without overlap (aa and bb can't share a letter). The shortest are aabb and bbaa.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: In the online equivalence tool, how do you write a ∪ λ?
choices: `a| ` with the space standing for λ
questions.explain: The tool has no λ symbol; an \*\*empty alternative\*\* is λ. So `a|` or `(a|)` (or `a?`). A space is ignored, so `a| ` is still a ∪ λ, but the space does nothing.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: What does the tool treat an \*\*empty\*\* input field as?
questions.explain: An empty field means λ. That's why in class, typing into only one field made the tool compare against λ.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: You enter `a|` and `a*`. What does the tool report?
choices: Accepted by first but not second: a
Accepted by second but not first: aa
Accepted by second but not first: [empty string]
questions.explain: λ and a are in both sets. The shortlex-first difference is aa: it belongs to the set described by a\* but not a ∪ λ.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: Which list is in shortlex order?
choices: λ, a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb
questions.explain: Shortlex: shorter strings first, then alphabetical within each length.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: When two expressions differ, the tool lists every string in the difference.
questions.explain: It shows only one string per direction: the shortlex-first string in the difference. Fixing that string makes it move on to the next one.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: The course's online regex-equivalence tool may be used during tests and reviews.
questions.explain: The instructor announced it (and repeated it on 2026-09-22). It is a checking aid; you still produce the answer yourself.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: Write (a ∪ bb)\*a in the tool's syntax (no spaces).
questions.explain: ∪ becomes `|`, concatenation is juxtaposition, and the star is `*`: `(a|bb)*a`.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: In the shell glob `*.pdf`, what does `*` mean?
choices: The Kleene star of the preceding symbol
Any string of characters, i.e. Σ\*
questions.explain: In a glob, `*` means any string of characters (Σ\*). It is not the Kleene star of the preceding symbol; globs have no general star operator.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: Programming-language regex engines with backreferences (e.g. `(a+)b\1`) can describe some languages that are not regular.
questions.explain: Backreferences go beyond ∅, λ, symbols, ∪, concatenation and star; `(a+)b\1` describes {aⁿbaⁿ}, which is not regular.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: A library regex search finds a match \*inside\* a string. How do you make it behave like a formal regular expression?
questions.explain: A formal regular expression describes whole strings, so use a full-match function or anchors `^…$`.

questions.category: The equivalence tool and everyday regex
questions.q: The tool says "Accepted by first but not second: w". How should you say this in course wording?
choices: w belongs to the set described by the first expression but not the second
questions.explain: "Accepted" is machine (automaton) vocabulary. For expressions, say w \*\*belongs to the set described by\*\* the first expression but not the second.
